## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dhammadhajajātaka* (Ja 384) is a tale from the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing recounted in the text, the Buddha related the story while dwelling at Jetavana regarding a deceitful monk, observing that this was not the first time the monk had engaged in deceit [SuttaCentral]. In the story, a hypocritical crow masquerades as a holy ascetic surviving on air alone; however, once left on its own, it secretly preys upon the eggs and young of other birds until it is eventually discovered and put to death [Anandajoti 2010]. The verse preserved in the collection illustrates deceitful appearances, comparing hypocritical wanderers who are outwardly splendid yet inwardly impure to a gilded clay earring or a gold-coated copper coin [Anandajoti 2010].
SuttaCentral identifies resembling parallels in the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 168, Dhp 169) and their wider parallels across the Buddhist tradition, including the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, the Patna Dharmapada, Sanskrit recensions of the *Udānavarga*, the *Avadānaśataka* (Avs 38), and Chinese translations such as T 210, T 212, and T 213 [SuttaCentral]. Furthermore, computational analysis by DharmaNexus detects Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary tradition, recording matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (specifically segments 3.1–6.4) and the *Dīghanikāya Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā* (segments 1.1–2.4) [DharmaNexus].
